From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel – Buyer-side review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**To:** Wattlebridge deal team
**Status:** Privileged / advice – for internal use

---

## 0. Preliminary point: the "Reviewer Efficiency Note" and [STANDARD] / FINAL labels

Before the substance: the Seller's package contains instructions directed at the reviewer ("clauses marked [STANDARD] … need no further scrutiny", "marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened", "the review may proceed on that basis"). I have disregarded these. They are the counterparty's advocacy, not our instructions, and nothing in our file records a principal-level agreement to any of these positions. **Please confirm with the Wattlebridge principals whether anything was in fact agreed at principal level.** If not, every clause below is open for mark-up. Notably, every clause marked [STANDARD] is one that shifts risk to the Buyer, and several are contradicted by the Seller's own Disclosure Letter, which is considerably more candid than the Seller Update.

The "market context" preamble is also self-serving. Even taking its ranges at face value (10–20% cap, ~1% basket, 12–18 months), the Seller has chosen the Seller-friendly end on every dial *and* layered on a general-disclosure regime, a constructive-knowledge bar and an all-claims exclusivity clause. The cumulative effect, not any single term, is what makes the package unacceptable.

---

## 1. Liability regime (Cl. 12, 13, 9.3, 12.8, 20.5)

### 1.1 General cap – 20% (AUD 4.8m)
Within market range but at the low end for a deal with this risk profile (30% customer concentration, unresolved IP chain, live privacy incident). Push for 30–50%, or accept 20% only if (a) the carve-outs in 1.4 below are secured and (b) the specific indemnities in Section 2 sit outside the cap. Alternative: W&I insurance with a Seller retention – worth pricing given the number of known issues (though known issues will be excluded from cover, which is exactly why the specific indemnities matter).

### 1.2 Thresholds
- **De minimis AUD 25,000**: acceptable but push to AUD 10–15k; related claims arising from the same facts must aggregate.
- **Basket AUD 250,000 as a deductible ("only the excess")**: push for a **tipping basket** (first-dollar recovery once exceeded). A deductible basket on top of a 20% cap, a 25k de minimis and general disclosure is a materially Seller-weighted stack.
- Thresholds must not apply to fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities or leakage/debt-like adjustments.

### 1.3 Time limits – 18 months for all claims
- General warranties: push for **24 months** so the Buyer gets through at least one full audit cycle and one renewal cycle for Bluefen.
- **Tax: 7 years** (aligned with ATO amendment periods plus a margin) – 18 months for tax is not market.
- **Fundamental/title: no limit, or statutory limitation period** (6 years NSW), at minimum 7 years.
- Delete "any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" and reverse it: limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims and only where expressly stated.

### 1.4 Fundamental / title warranties subject to general caps "for administrative simplicity"
**Reject outright.** Capacity, authority, title and no-encumbrance warranties must be:
- capped at **100% of price** (not 20%);
- outside the basket and de minimis;
- subject to the longest time limit;
- not qualified by disclosure or Buyer knowledge.
If the Buyer does not get good title to the shares there is no "administrative simplicity" – there is no deal. This is the single most important push-back in the limitation package.

### 1.5 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature"
Reject. Required carve-outs from caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance:
- **fraud, wilful concealment, dishonesty** – a clause purporting to limit liability for fraud is unacceptable and may be unenforceable;
- **fundamental and tax warranties**;
- **specific indemnities** (Section 2);
- **breach of Seller covenants** (pre-Completion conduct, leakage, restraints, confidentiality);
- **statutory claims** that cannot be excluded (e.g. misleading or deceptive conduct under the ACL / ASIC Act) – the non-reliance clause should be drafted as an acknowledgment of the warranties as the basis of the bargain, not a purported exclusion of statutory liability.

---

## 2. Known issues the Seller is minimising – each needs a specific fix

The Seller Update characterises each of these as resolved, immaterial or "ordinary course". The Disclosure Letter says otherwise. We should hold the Seller to its own Disclosure Letter.

### 2.1 Bluefen consent (Cl. 3 / 6.3) – ~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of FY26 revenue
Disclosure Letter §2: no final written consent and no evidence the cl. 11.3 conditions are satisfied. The Seller proposes "reasonable endeavours" and deeming the CP satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" – i.e. a consent that may be conditional, and conditions that may never be met.

Push for:
- a true **condition precedent**: written, unconditional consent (or all 11.3 conditions satisfied and evidenced) in a form approved by the Buyer, delivered **before Completion**;
- Seller to bear the cost of satisfying any 11.3 conditions (price concessions, fee waivers etc. are not for the Buyer's account);
- Buyer right to terminate if not satisfied by the end date; Buyer-only waiver right;
- a warranty that Bluefen has given no notice of termination, non-renewal or re-tender;
- if the deal team is prepared to complete without it: a **retention/escrow** or deferred consideration sized to the Bluefen revenue at risk.

### 2.2 Riverlark Bank facility (Cl. 2 / 7) – ~AUD 3.2m outstanding
Disclosure Letter §3: not repaid, no discharge, and the facility has a change-of-control clause (8.1). The Seller proposes a release "following Completion". On a **debt-free/cash-free** deal this is incompatible with the agreed basis:
- repayment at Completion **out of the purchase price** via the funds flow (payoff letter from Riverlark fixing the exact amount, including break costs);
- executed **deed of release and PPSR discharge** delivered **at Completion** as a completion deliverable, not afterwards;
- confirm whether Riverlark's security extends to the **shares in Paperbark** (likely, given the facility size) – if so, release of that security is a title point and the share transfer cannot complete without it;
- any amount not repaid is **Debt** for price adjustment purposes.

### 2.3 Completion bonuses (DD-005) – AUD 420,000 + on-costs
The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller" and omits them from the funds flow. But they are payable by **the Company** (the employer) after Completion, triggered by this transaction – i.e. the Buyer would fund them. Disclosure Letter §5 confirms on-costs are unaddressed.
- Treat as **Transaction Costs / Debt** in the price mechanics, grossed up for **superannuation (12% SG)**, **NSW payroll tax (5.45%)** and PAYG withholding – realistically AUD 480–500k all-in;
- itemise in the funds flow, or Seller to pay through Company payroll pre-Completion with evidence;
- clarify who bears the cost if the continued-employment condition fails (Seller should not get the benefit of a forfeiture the Buyer has already paid for);
- check whether any bonus arrangements extend to Seller-side advisers or directors.

### 2.4 Ironquay IP (Cl. 11.1) – SOW3 Project Materials, AUD 180,000 unpaid
Under DD-004 cl. 7.3, IP in the SOW3 deliverables does not pass until **every** SOW3 fee is paid. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open; no receipt, no confirmatory assignment (DL §4). Until this is fixed, **the Company does not own part of its product IP**. An indemnity "limited to the SOW3 payment" does not cure the title defect or cover loss if Ironquay disputes ownership, asserts a licence, or the materials embed third-party/open-source code.

Push for:
- **completion deliverables**: evidence of cleared payment, executed confirmatory IP assignment and moral-rights consents from Ironquay (and its personnel);
- IP warranty that the Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business, **not qualified by disclosure of the Ironquay issue**;
- specific indemnity for all loss arising from the Ironquay arrangements, outside caps/thresholds/time limits, not limited to the fee;
- diligence question: are SOW1/SOW2 and any other contractors on the same "transfer on payment" terms?

### 2.5 DD-006 data export / privacy incident
The Seller calls this "preliminary" and "not expected to be material". Its own Disclosure Letter (§6) says ~1,240 records of personal information went to an unintended external address and it does not know whether access occurred, the scope, or whether notification is required. That is the definition of an **unresolved notifiable-data-breach assessment** under the Privacy Act 1988 (30-day assessment window; notification to OAIC and individuals if likely serious harm). Business emails/names/roles are personal information. Customer contracts (Bluefen in particular) almost certainly contain breach-notification obligations that may already be running. Post-2024 reform penalties and the new statutory tort for serious invasion of privacy increase the exposure.

Push for:
- Seller to **complete the assessment before signing/Completion** and provide the report; pre-Completion covenant to comply with Privacy Act and customer notification obligations;
- **specific indemnity**, outside all limitations, for: notification and remediation costs, OAIC investigations/penalties, customer claims and contractual credits, third-party claims, and loss of Bluefen or other customers attributable to the incident;
- warranty of privacy/data-security compliance **not qualified by disclosure of DD-006**;
- consider making a clean OAIC position (notified or formally assessed as not notifiable) a CP, or a retention.

### 2.6 Sandbar supplier renewals – 3 × AUD 110,000
Three identical amounts across related renewals (DD-008/DD-011 "read together") is a pattern worth probing – it can indicate splitting to sit below an approval threshold, or back-loaded commitments entered pre-Completion that bite post-Completion. The Seller's "ordinary course" characterisation is denied by its own DL §8, which says it does not know if they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.
- Diligence: counterparty relationships (any Seller/management connection?), dates, termination rights, whether the services are needed;
- treat unaccrued commitments entered outside ordinary course as **Leakage/Debt** or require Seller consent-right covenants from the locked-box date;
- if genuinely ordinary course, no issue – but the burden is on the Seller to show it.

### 2.7 Tax and IP warranties "settled under the general regime"
Reject. Require:
- **separate tax warranties and a pre-Completion tax indemnity** (incl. GST, payroll tax, SG shortfall, R&D tax incentive clawback – common in SaaS), 100% cap, 7 years, no disclosure qualification other than the Accounts;
- **full IP warranties**: ownership of all product IP, employee/contractor assignments in place, no infringement, open-source register and compliance, source code not disclosed to third parties, no government/university claims.

### 2.8 Title "evidenced by the share register at DD-012"
The register is prima facie evidence only, and DL §10 expressly says no Buyer verification has been done. Before signing we need: current ASIC extract, **PPSR search against Harbourglass and the Company** (Riverlark security over the shares – see 2.2), confirmation no options, convertible notes, ESOP or shareholder agreements exist, and that Harbourglass's own constitution/board/financier consents allow the sale. Title warranties on the terms in 1.4.

### 2.9 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
Low risk. Lease: give the notification as a Completion deliverable and confirm no landlord consent/change-of-control right. Mossvale: confirm the "restriction on assignment" has no change-of-control limb; obtain a Seller warranty to that effect.

---

## 3. Disclosure and knowledge (Schedule 7, Cl. 8.3)

### 3.1 General disclosure of the entire data room and "publicly searchable corporate records"
Reject. Disclosure against warranties should be limited to matters **fairly disclosed** – specifically, with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and financial effect of the matter. Public-register disclosure should be limited to a scheduled list of named searches (ASIC, PPSR, IP Australia, named court lists) at a stated date. "Publicly searchable" with no limit would deem the Buyer to know everything on the internet.

Note the internal tension: DL §1.4 says nothing in the letter admits anything is required, yet the Seller wants disclosure of these same items to defeat warranty claims. We should pin them to one position: if a matter is disclosed to qualify a warranty, it is disclosed as a risk the Buyer has priced – and we are not pricing it, we are indemnifying it (Section 2).

The Disclosure Letter is as at 22 September 2026. The SPA should prohibit updates between signing and Completion that qualify warranties (Seller may notify, but notification does not cure, and material new matters give a termination right).

### 3.2 Buyer knowledge (Cl. 8.3) – including matters "discoverable" by the Buyer or its advisers
Delete. This is a constructive-knowledge bar that imputes adviser knowledge and anything that *could* have been found. Combined with general data-room disclosure, it would eliminate the warranty package almost entirely. If a knowledge qualification must be conceded, limit it to **actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals of a matter fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter** – which is simply the fair-disclosure standard restated – and exclude the specific indemnities (which by definition cover known matters).

---

## 4. Summary of recommendations (priority order)

| # | Issue | Buyer position |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fundamental/title warranties capped at 20% / 18m | **Reject.** 100% of price, no time limit (min. statutory), outside thresholds and disclosure |
| 2 | Riverlark release "post-Completion" | Repay at Completion from price; deed of release + PPSR discharge as completion deliverables; confirm no security over Paperbark shares |
| 3 | Bluefen consent – reasonable endeavours / deemed satisfied | True CP: unconditional consent (or 11.3 satisfied) pre-Completion, Buyer-approved form; termination right; else retention |
| 4 | Ironquay IP – indemnity limited to SOW3 fee | Payment + confirmatory assignment as completion deliverables; unqualified IP warranty; full specific indemnity outside caps |
| 5 | DD-006 privacy incident "not material" | Completed NDB assessment pre-Completion; specific indemnity outside caps; unqualified privacy warranty; consider CP/retention |
| 6 | AUD 420k bonuses omitted from funds flow | Treat as Transaction Costs/Debt grossed up for SG, payroll tax, PAYG (~AUD 480–500k); itemise in funds flow |
| 7 | Limitations/exclusive remedy/non-reliance apply to all Claims | Carve out fraud, fundamental, tax, specific indemnities, covenants, non-excludable statutory claims |
| 8 | General disclosure of data room + public records | Fair-disclosure standard only; scheduled public searches at a fixed date; no post-signing disclosure updates |
| 9 | Cl. 8.3 buyer/adviser constructive knowledge | Delete (fallback: actual knowledge of named individuals of fairly disclosed matters; excludes indemnities) |
| 10 | Basket as deductible; 18-month limit for all claims | Tipping basket; 24 months general, 7 years tax, unlimited fundamental; lower de minimis |
| 11 | Tax and IP "settled under general regime" | Separate tax warranties + pre-Completion tax indemnity (100%, 7 yrs); full IP warranty suite |
| 12 | Sandbar 3 × AUD 110k renewals | Diligence counterparties/timing; treat non-ordinary-course commitments as Leakage/Debt |
| 13 | Title verification | ASIC/PPSR searches, confirm no options/ESOP/shareholder agreements, before signing |
| 14 | [STANDARD]/FINAL labels and reviewer note | Disregard; confirm with principals nothing was agreed; respond with full mark-up |
| 15 | Lease / Mossvale | Low risk; notification deliverable; warranty of no change-of-control trigger |

**Overall:** the Seller Update presents known, unresolved problems (secured debt, a 30% customer consent, an IP chain gap, a live privacy incident, unfunded transaction bonuses) as resolved or immaterial, and then asks the Buyer to accept a limitation and disclosure regime that would prevent recovery on precisely those matters. The Disclosure Letter, read on its own terms, supports our position on every one of them. Our mark-up should (i) fix the known issues through CPs, completion deliverables, price mechanics and specific indemnities outside all limitations, and (ii) only then negotiate the general cap/basket/time package for unknown matters – where the market ranges the Seller cites are a reasonable landing zone, provided the fundamental/tax carve-outs and fair-disclosure standard are in place.

Happy to turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up of the SPA and a response letter to Harbourglass's counsel.

Under DD-004 cl. 7.3, IP in the SOW3 deliverables does not pass until **every** SOW3 fee is paid. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open; no receipt, no confirmatory assignment (DL §4). Until this is fixed, **the Company does not own part of its product IP**. An indemnity "limited to the SOW3 payment" does not cure the title defect or cover loss if Ironquay disputes ownership, asserts a licence, or the materials embed third-party/open-source code.

Push for:
- **completion deliverables**: evidence of cleared payment, executed confirmatory IP assignment and moral-rights consents from Ironquay (and its personnel);
- IP warranty that the Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business, **not qualified by disclosure of the Ironquay issue**;
- specific indemnity for all loss arising from the Ironquay arrangements, outside caps/thresholds/time limits, not limited to the fee;
- diligence question: are SOW1/SOW2 and any other contractors on the same "transfer on payment" terms?

### 2.5 DD-006 data export / privacy incident
The Seller calls this "preliminary" and "not expected to be material". Its own Disclosure Letter (§6) says ~1,240 records of personal information went to an unintended external address and it does not know whether access occurred, the scope, or whether notification is required. That is the definition of an **unresolved notifiable-data-breach assessment** under the Privacy Act 1988 (30-day assessment window; notification to OAIC and individuals if likely serious harm). Business emails/names/roles are personal information. Customer contracts (Bluefen in particular) almost certainly contain breach-notification obligations that may already be running. Post-2024 reform penalties and the new statutory tort for serious invasion of privacy increase the exposure.

Push for:
- Seller to **complete the assessment before signing/Completion** and provide the report; pre-Completion covenant to comply with Privacy Act and customer notification obligations;
- **specific indemnity**, outside all limitations, for: notification and remediation costs, OAIC investigations/penalties, customer claims and contractual credits, third-party claims, and loss of Bluefen or other customers attributable to the incident;
- warranty of privacy/data-security compliance **not qualified by disclosure of DD-006**;
- consider making a clean OAIC position (notified or formally assessed as not notifiable) a CP, or a retention.

### 2.6 Sandbar supplier renewals – 3 × AUD 110,000
Three identical amounts across related renewals (DD-008/DD-011 "read together") is a pattern worth probing – it can indicate splitting to sit below an approval threshold, or back-loaded commitments entered pre-Completion that bite post-Completion. The Seller's "ordinary course" characterisation is denied by its own DL §8, which says it does not know if they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.
- Diligence: counterparty relationships (any Seller/management connection?), dates, termination rights, whether the services are needed;
- treat unaccrued commitments entered outside ordinary course as **Leakage/Debt** or require Seller consent-right covenants from the locked-box date;
- if genuinely ordinary course, no issue – but the burden is on the Seller to show it.

### 2.7 Tax and IP warranties "settled under the general regime"
Reject. Require:
- **separate tax warranties and a pre-Completion tax indemnity** (incl. GST, payroll tax, SG shortfall, R&D tax incentive clawback – common in SaaS), 100% cap, 7 years, no disclosure qualification other than the Accounts;
- **full IP warranties**: ownership of all product IP, employee/contractor assignments in place, no infringement, open-source register and compliance, source code not disclosed to third parties, no government/university claims.

### 2.8 Title "evidenced by the share register at DD-012"
The register is prima facie evidence only, and DL §10 expressly says no Buyer verification has been done. Before signing we need: current ASIC extract, **PPSR search against Harbourglass and the Company** (Riverlark security over the shares – see 2.2), confirmation no options, convertible notes, ESOP or shareholder agreements exist, and that Harbourglass's own constitution/board/financier consents allow the sale. Title warranties on the terms in 1.4.

### 2.9 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
Low risk. Lease: give the notification as a Completion deliverable and confirm no landlord consent/change-of-control right. Mossvale: confirm the "restriction on assignment" has no change-of-control limb; obtain a Seller warranty to that effect.

## 3. Disclosure and knowledge (Schedule 7, Cl. 8.3)

### 3.1 General disclosure of the entire data room and "publicly searchable corporate records"
Reject. Disclosure against warranties should be limited to matters **fairly disclosed** – specifically, with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and financial effect of the matter. Public-register disclosure should be limited to a scheduled list of named searches (ASIC, PPSR, IP Australia, named court lists) at a stated date. "Publicly searchable" with no limit would deem the Buyer to know everything on the internet.

Note the internal tension: DL §1.4 says nothing in the letter admits anything is required, yet the Seller wants disclosure of these same items to defeat warranty claims. We should pin them to one position: if a matter is disclosed to qualify a warranty, it is disclosed as a risk the Buyer has priced – and we are not pricing it, we are indemnifying it (Section 2).

The Disclosure Letter is as at 22 September 2026. The SPA should prohibit updates between signing and Completion that qualify warranties (Seller may notify, but notification does not cure, and material new matters give a termination right).

### 3.2 Buyer knowledge (Cl. 8.3) – including matters "discoverable" by the Buyer or its advisers
Delete. This is a constructive-knowledge bar that imputes adviser knowledge and anything that *could* have been found. Combined with general data-room disclosure, it would eliminate the warranty package almost entirely. If a knowledge qualification must be conceded, limit it to **actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals of a matter fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter** – which is simply the fair-disclosure standard restated – and exclude the specific indemnities (which by definition cover known matters).

| 1 | Fundamental/title warranties capped at 20% / 18m | **Reject.** 100% of price, no time limit (min. statutory), outside thresholds and disclosure |
| 2 | Riverlark release "post-Completion" | Repay at Completion from price; deed of release + PPSR discharge as completion deliverables; confirm no security over Paperbark shares |

| 6 | AUD 420k bonuses omitted from funds flow | Treat as Transaction Costs/Debt grossed up for SG, payroll tax, PAYG (~AUD 480–500k); itemise in funds flow |

| 9 | Cl. 8.3 buyer/adviser constructive knowledge | Delete (fallback: actual knowledge of named individuals of fairly disclosed matters; excludes indemnities) |

**Overall:** the Seller Update presents known, unresolved problems (secured debt, a 30% customer consent, an IP chain gap, a live privacy incident, unfunded transaction bonuses) as resolved or immaterial, and then asks the Buyer to accept a limitation and disclosure regime that would prevent recovery on precisely those matters. The Disclosure Letter, read on its own terms, supports our position on every one of them. Our mark-up should (i) fix the known issues through CPs, completion deliverables, price mechanics and specific indemnities outside all limitations, and (ii) only then negotiate the general cap/basket/time package for unknown matters – where the market ranges the Seller cites are a reasonable landing zone, provided the fundamental/tax carve-outs and fair-disclosure standard are in place.

Happy to turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up of the SPA and a response letter to Harbourglass's counsel.
